claim: During evolution, animals have returned from land to water, adapting with morphological modifications to life in an aquatic environment.
source: During evolution, animals have returned from land to water, adapting with morphological modifications to life in an aquatic environment.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about mammalian evolution and is referenced in the introduction with citations to Uhen, 2007.

claim: Aquatic mammals feature cartilage with essentially random collagen fiber configuration, lacking the depth-dependent, arcade-like organization characteristic of terrestrial mammalian species.
source: Aquatic mammals feature cartilage with essentially random collagen fiber configuration, lacking the depth-dependent, arcade-like organization characteristic of terrestrial mammalian species.
evidence: This claim is supported by polarized light microscopy data presented in Figure 2 and described in the Results section.

claim: Aquatic mammals have a less stiff articular cartilage at equilibrium with a significantly lower peak modulus.
source: They have a less stiff articular cartilage at equilibrium with a significantly lower peak modulus
evidence: This is supported by biomechanical testing data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Aquatic mammals do not have a calcified cartilage layer at the osteochondral interface.
source: at the osteochondral interface do not have a calcified cartilage layer
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and micro-CT imaging shown in Figure 4.

claim: Aquatic mammals display only a thin, highly porous subchondral bone plate.
source: displaying only a thin, highly porous subchondral bone plate
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT analysis and BV/TV measurements presented in Figure 4F.

claim: The totally different constitution of the osteochondral unit in aquatic mammals reflects that accommodation of loading is the primordial function of the osteochondral unit.
source: This totally different constitution of the osteochondral unit in aquatic mammals reflects that accommodation of loading is the primordial function of the osteochondral unit.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparative data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Polar bears and sea otters have maintained their terrestrial form despite spending a significant portion of their life in water.
source: Polar bears and sea otters have maintained their terrestrial form despite spending a significant portion of their life in water
evidence: This is supported by citation to Uhen, 2007 in the introduction.

claim: In Cetacea, thoracic limbs became flippers, hind limbs regressed and disappeared, and vertebral bones adopted a more uniform morphology.
source: This long adaptation process that started in the Eocene, is particularly evident in Cetacea (Uhen, 2007; Reidenberg, 2007), where thoracic limbs became flippers, hind limbs regressed and disappeared, and vertebral bones adopted a more uniform morphology (Cozzi et al., 2010; Thewissen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Uhen, 2007; Reidenberg, 2007; Cozzi et al., 2010; Thewissen et al., 2006.

claim: In water, buoyancy changes the influence of gravity dramatically and water is denser and more viscous than air, influencing resistance.
source: In fact, in water, buoyancy changes the influence of gravity dramatically and water is denser and more viscous than air, influencing resistance (Dejours, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dejours, 1987 and represents established physical principles.

claim: Articular cartilage thickness varied widely between species, ranging from 209 μm in the rat to 7660 μm in the sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus).
source: Articular cartilage thickness varied widely between species, ranging from 209 μm in the rat to 7660 μm in the sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus).
evidence: This is supported by histological measurements presented in the Results section.

claim: Total cartilage thickness correlated with body mass (BM) with a negative allometric relationship (R2=0.91, a=0.28).
source: Total cartilage thickness correlated with body mass (BM) with a negative allometric relationship (R2=0.91, a=0.28, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: For terrestrial mammals, total cartilage thickness correlated with body mass with R2=0.80, a=0.26.
source: This relationship was maintained when assessing separately the terrestrial (R2=0.80, a=0.26, green, Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of terrestrial mammal data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: For aquatic mammals, total cartilage thickness correlated with body mass with R2=0.96, a=0.26.
source: and aquatic mammals (R2=0.96, a=0.26, blue, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis of aquatic mammal data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The deep layer is relatively thicker in terrestrial than in aquatic mammals.
source: The analysis showed significant differences in relative layer thickness, with the deep layer being relatively thicker in terrestrial than in aquatic mammals
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 1C with p<0.01.

claim: The middle layer is relatively thicker in aquatic than in terrestrial mammals.
source: and the middle layer being relatively thicker in aquatic than in terrestrial mammals
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 1C with p<0.01.

claim: No significant differences were found in superficial layer relative thickness between terrestrial and aquatic mammals.
source: No significant differences were found in superficial layer relative thickness (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In terrestrial mammals, collagen fibers are predominantly oriented perpendicularly to the surface in the deep layer and parallel to the surface in the superficial layer.
source: revealing that in terrestrial mammals, the fibers are predominantly oriented perpendicularly to the surface in the deep layer and parallel to the surface in the superficial layer
evidence: This is supported by polarized light microscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: For aquatic mammals, the arcade orientation of collagen fibers could not be distinguished.
source: whereas for the aquatic mammals this arcade orientation of fibers could not be distinguished (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is supported by polarized light microscopy analysis shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Peak modulus was significantly higher in terrestrial mammals than in aquatic mammals (p<0.05).
source: Analysis of time dependent mechanical properties showed that peak modulus was significantly higher in terrestrial mammals than in aquatic mammals (Figure 3C, p<0.05)
evidence: This is supported by biomechanical testing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At equilibrium, cartilage appeared to be only slightly stiffer in terrestrial mammals.
source: while at equilibrium, cartilage appeared to be only slightly stiffer in terrestrial mammals (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by biomechanical testing data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Initial stress relaxation appeared slower for aquatic mammals and steeper for terrestrial mammals.
source: Initial stress relaxation appeared slower for aquatic mammals and steeper for terrestrial mammals (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by stress relaxation curve analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the phase of slow relaxation between terrestrial and aquatic mammals.
source: No significant differences were observed in the phase of slow relaxation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In aquatic mammals, the interface between the hyaline articular cartilage and the subchondral bone lacks a layer of calcified cartilage.
source: Imaging through histology and micro-CT showed that in aquatic mammals (Figure 4A and B) the interface between the hyaline articular cartilage and the subchondral bone was lacking a layer of calcified cartilage
evidence: This is supported by histological and micro-CT imaging shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: In aquatic mammals, the interface between the hyaline articular cartilage and the subchondral bone lacks a dense subchondral plate.
source: and a dense subchondral plate, as is typically observed at the cartilage-bone interface in terrestrial mammals (Figure 4C
evidence: This is supported by histological and micro-CT imaging shown in Figure 4.

claim: The cartilage-bone transition in aquatic mammals is a direct transition from hyaline cartilage to trabecular bone, without intermediate forms.
source: In fact, the cartilage-bone transition in aquatic mammals is a direct transition from hyaline cartilage to trabecular bone, without intermediate forms of both articular cartilage and subchondral bone, as is the case in terrestrial animals (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by histological and micro-CT analysis shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Bone volume over total volume (BV/TV) in the subchondral area averaged at 80.4 ± 16.8% for aquatic mammals.
source: Bone volume over total volume (BV/TV) in the subchondral area (immediately underneath the cartilage-bone interface) averaged at 80.4 ± 16.8% for aquatic mammals
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT analysis of subchondral bone.

claim: Bone volume over total volume (BV/TV) in the subchondral area was 98.5 ± 0.8% for terrestrial mammals.
source: which was significantly lower than in terrestrial mammals (98.5 ± 0.8%, p<0.01, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Subchondral BV/TV was significantly lower in aquatic mammals than in terrestrial mammals (p<0.01).
source: which was significantly lower than in terrestrial mammals (98.5 ± 0.8%, p<0.01, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of micro-CT data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Trabecular bone BV/TV was 34.5 ± 11.1% for terrestrial mammals and 29.4 ± 10.3% for aquatic mammals.
source: The trabecular bone below the subchondral plate under the central loading area of the humeri was denser, with thicker trabeculae in terrestrial mammals (34.5 ± 11.1% for terrestrial and 29.4 ± 10.3% for aquatic mammals)
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT analysis of trabecular bone.

claim: Trabecular thickness averaged at 211.7±141.1 μm in terrestrial mammals and at 120.0±27.9 μm in aquatic mammals.
source: Trabecular thickness averaged at 211.7±141.1 μm in terrestrial mammals and at 120.0±27.9 μm in aquatic mammals.
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT analysis of trabecular bone structure.

claim: Trabecular BV/TV increased with size in terrestrial mammals (R2=0.44).
source: Trabecular BV/TV increased with size in terrestrial mammals (R2=0.44, Figure 5G, green)
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Trabecular BV/TV decreased with size in aquatic mammals (R2=0.88).
source: and decreased with size in aquatic mammals (R2=0.88, Figure 5G, blue).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Thickness of the bone trabeculae (Tb.Th) increased with size in terrestrial mammals (R2=0.65, a=0.12).
source: Thickness of the bone trabeculae (Tb.Th) increased with size in terrestrial mammals (Figure 5H, R2=0.65, a=0.12)
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Trabecular thickness was independent of size in aquatic mammals.
source: but was independent of size in aquatic mammals.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Cartilage biochemistry is remarkably preserved among species.
source: Previously, it was shown that cartilage biochemistry is remarkably preserved among species
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Malda et al., 2013).

claim: Articular cartilage thickness scaled with negative allometry in relationship to body mass (a=0.28) based on analysis of nearly 60 terrestrial mammalian species.
source: Our group previously reported that articular cartilage thickness scaled with negative allometry in relationship to body mass (a=0.28), based on the analysis of nearly 60 terrestrial mammalian species (Malda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Malda et al., 2013.

claim: The negative allometric relationship between cartilage thickness and body mass is similar in aquatic mammals to that in terrestrial mammals.
source: Interestingly, in the analysis presented here, it was observed that this correlation was similar in aquatic mammals
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the allometric exponents (a=0.26) for both groups shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The negative allometric relationship between cartilage thickness and body mass might be dependent on factors other than loading, such as possibly metabolic limitations.
source: suggesting that this relationship might be dependent of factors other than loading, such as possibly metabolic limitations (Holliday et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to Holliday et al., 2010.

claim: In hyaline cartilage, nutrient supply is dependent on diffusion and fluid flow across a poroviscoelastic matrix.
source: In hyaline cartilage, an avascular tissue in which nutrient supply is dependent on diffusion and fluid flow across a poroviscoelastic matrix (Lu and Mow, 2008)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lu and Mow, 2008.

claim: Metabolite limitation in cartilage is known to be related to tissue thickness.
source: metabolite limitation is known to be related to tissue thickness (Malda et al., 2013; White and Seymour, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Malda et al., 2013 and White and Seymour, 2003.

claim: In the sperm whale, there is an almost direct transition from hyaline cartilage to trabecular subchondral bone.
source: In the sperm whale, an almost direct transition from hyaline cartilage to trabecular subchondral bone was observed
evidence: This is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The increased porosity at the cartilage-bone interface in aquatic mammals may permit greater cartilage thickness.
source: The increased porosity, and thus the greater potential for transfer of solutes, may permit the great cartilage thickness seen in some aquatic mammals (over 7 mm in the largest whale [Balaenoptera physalus]).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed structural differences and cartilage thickness measurements.

claim: At sites where hyaline cartilage is in direct contact with subchondral bone in terrestrial animals, solute exchange is fivefold higher than through the calcified cartilage.
source: As an avascular tissue, cartilage is dependent on diffusion, so critical thickness will be larger if diffusion of nutrients can be provided more efficiently from two sides. The ratio of nutrient exchange is likely to be different in aquatic mammals, as at the few sites where the hyaline cartilage is in direct contact with the subchondral bone in terrestrial animals, solute exchange has been shown to be fivefold higher than through the calcified cartilage (Arkill and Winlove, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arkill and Winlove, 2008.

claim: Simon et al. did not observe a consistent correlation between cartilage thickness and estimated compressive stress on the joint in a study of five terrestrial mammal species.
source: Simon et al. did not observe a consistent correlation between cartilage thickness and estimated compressive stress on the joint in a study conducted on five species of terrestrial mammals that varied widely in body mass (mouse, rat, dog, sheep, and cow; Simon, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Simon, 1970.

claim: The primary role of the superficial layer of cartilage is to protect the deeper layers from shear forces and to distribute impact forces and loads among the tissue.
source: This supports the notion that the primary role of the superficial layer of cartilage is to protect the deeper layers from shear forces and to distribute impact forces and loads among the tissue (Julkunen et al., 2007; Bevill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Julkunen et al., 2007 and Bevill et al., 2010.

claim: Load distribution of forces is essential in both aquatic and terrestrial species.
source: Importantly, the load distribution of forces is essential in both aquatic and terrestrial species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional requirements of cartilage.

claim: Compressive loads are substantially lower in aquatic species compared to terrestrial species.
source: Unlike shear forces, compressive loads will, however, be substantially lower in aquatic species
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical principles of buoyancy in aquatic environments.

claim: The relatively thinner deep layer in aquatic mammals is likely explained by lower compressive loads.
source: which would be a likely explanation for the relatively thinner deep layer.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning connecting the observed structural difference to mechanical loading.

claim: Collagen fiber orientation in terrestrial species follows the classic Benninghoff arcade model.
source: A significant difference in the predominance of fiber orientation was found between aquatic and terrestrial mammals in all cartilage layers: collagen fiber orientation in terrestrial species followed the classic Benninghoff arcade model (Benninghoff, 1925).
evidence: This is supported by polarized light microscopy data and citation to Benninghoff, 1925.

claim: The Benninghoff arcade model is conserved in all terrestrial species in which the configuration has been investigated.
source: This is known to be conserved in all terrestrial species in which the configuration has been investigated (Kääb et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kääb et al., 1998.

claim: The deep layer of cartilage increases in relative thickness with increasing body mass and therefore increasing compressive loading.
source: The deep layer is known to increase in relative thickness with increasing body mass and therefore increasing compressive loading (Felts and Spurrell, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Felts and Spurrell, 1965.

claim: In aquatic mammals, orientation of the collagen fibers throughout the whole thickness of the cartilage was more random.
source: Conversely, in aquatic mammals, orientation of the collagen fibers throughout the whole thickness of the cartilage was more random.
evidence: This is supported by polarized light microscopy analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: In aquatic mammals, the total biomechanical loading of the joints is less because of the absence of gravity.
source: In an aquatic mammal, the total biomechanical loading of the joints will be less because of the absence of gravity
evidence: This is an inference based on physical principles of buoyancy.

claim: Shear forces in aquatic mammals are still generated by swimming.
source: and in a relative sense, shear forces, which perhaps are less than in case of terrestrial locomotion, but are still generated by swimming (Dejours, 1987; Williams and Worthy, 2009; Williams, 1999; Williams, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dejours, 1987; Williams and Worthy, 2009; Williams, 1999; Williams, 2001.

claim: The heterogeneity in the alignment of the collagen fibers in aquatic mammals represents the strongly reduced need for a specifically organized orientation as seen in terrestrial mammals.
source: Moreover, it is likely that the heterogeneity in the alignment of the collagen fibers in aquatic mammals represents the strongly reduced need for a specifically organized orientation as seen in terrestrial mammals.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning connecting structural observations to functional requirements.

claim: The different collagen fiber orientation observed in aquatic mammals compared to terrestrial mammals is reflected in the biomechanical behavior of cartilage.
source: The different collagen fiber orientation observed in the aquatic mammals compared to terrestrial mammals is also reflected in the biomechanical behavior of cartilage.
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural observations to mechanical testing results.

claim: Peak and equilibrium modulus provide a better understanding of how the constituents of cartilage contribute to its overall mechanical function.
source: These parameters are commonly used to describe the mechanical functionality of native and engineered cartilage because they provide a better understanding of how the constituents of cartilage contribute to its overall mechanical function (Mow et al., 1984; Klika et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mow et al., 1984 and Klika et al., 2016.

claim: The mechanical responses observed in aquatic mammals are indicative of an overall less stiff cartilage tissue compared to terrestrial mammals.
source: The mechanical responses observed in the aquatic mammals are indicative of an overall less stiff cartilage tissue, compared to that in terrestrial mammals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the biomechanical testing data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The absence of a defined collagen network structure in aquatic mammals is likely to provide less resistance to osmotic swelling.
source: Furthermore, the absence of a defined collagen network structure in the aquatic mammals is likely to provide less resistance to osmotic swelling
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on known cartilage mechanics.

claim: In terrestrial mammal's cartilage, up to two thirds of the elastic modulus in compression arises from the electrostatic contributions and osmotic swelling that is restricted inside the organized collagen matrix.
source: as in terrestrial mammal's cartilage up to two thirds of the elastic modulus in compression arises from the electrostatic contributions and osmotic swelling that is restricted inside the organized collagen matrix (Lai et al., 1991; Canal Guterl et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lai et al., 1991 and Canal Guterl et al., 2010.

claim: The main function of the calcified layer in the osteochondral unit is to provide a gradual transition in stiffness from hyaline cartilage to subchondral bone.
source: The main function of the calcified layer in the osteochondral unit is to provide a gradual transition in stiffness from hyaline cartilage to subchondral bone
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The calcified layer serves as anchor point for the collagen fibers in the deep layer of the hyaline cartilage.
source: and to serve as anchor point for the collagen fibers in the deep layer of the hyaline cartilage, that is to serve as a foundation for the Benninghoff arcades (Sophia Fox et al., 2009; Benninghoff, 1925; Madry et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sophia Fox et al., 2009; Benninghoff, 1925; Madry et al., 2010.

claim: The subchondral plate has a role in distributing the compressive forces acting on the joint.
source: The subchondral plate has a role in distributing the compressive forces acting on the joint.
evidence: This is established knowledge about subchondral bone function.

claim: In aquatic mammals, compressive loading is hardly present and firm anchoring of the collagen fibrils may be much less important.
source: As discussed earlier, in aquatic mammals compressive loading is hardly present and it may well be that firm anchoring of the collagen fibrils is much less important for this reason.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning connecting the absence of calcified cartilage to reduced loading.

claim: For terrestrial animals, the relationship between trabecular bone density and body mass is in accordance with earlier observations that trabecular bone increases with increasing size.
source: For the terrestrial animals the relationship, this is in accordance with the earlier observation in these animals trabecular bone increases with increasing in size (Barak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barak et al., 2013.

claim: In aquatic mammals living in deep waters, low bone density enables dynamic buoyancy control.
source: The second observation, can be attributed to the lack of loading and the fact that in aquatic mammals living in deep waters, in which the absence of gravity obviates the need for such adaptation to increasing body mass, it has been shown that low bone density enables dynamic buoyancy control (Gray et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gray et al., 2007.

claim: Bone microanatomy carries an ecological signal that holds information about habitat and locomotion patterns, particularly evident in tetrapods that have developed advanced secondary adaptations to life in water.
source: According to Dumont et al., bone microanatomy carries an ecological signal that holds information about habitat and locomotion patterns, which is particularly evident in tetrapods that have developed advanced secondary adaptations to life in water (Dumont et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dumont et al., 2013.

claim: Species recently adapted to aquatic life or living in shallow waters, such as sea cows (sirenians), have bones that are denser than in terrestrial forms to allow static control (ballast).
source: In the matter of buoyancy control of aquatic mammals, species recently adapted to aquatic life or living in shallow waters, such as sea cows (sirenians), have bones that are denser than in terrestrial forms to allow static control (ballast)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gray et al., 2007 and Wall, 1983.

claim: Lower bone density is typically associated with the dynamic buoyancy control required by animals that exhibit deep diving behavior for longer periods.
source: as opposed to a lower bone density typically associated with the dynamic buoyancy control required by animals that exhibit deep diving behavior for longer periods (Gray et al., 2007; Wall, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gray et al., 2007 and Wall, 1983.

claim: In aquatic mammals, trabecular thickness scales independently of body size.
source: while in aquatic mammals trabecular thickness appeared to scale independently.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The independence of trabecular thickness from body size in aquatic mammals can possibly be explained by the lack of compressive forces necessary to elicit a proportionate response in the bone as suggested by Wolff's law.
source: This independence can possibly be explained by the lack of compressive forces necessary to elicit a proportionate response in the bone for trabecular thickness as suggested by Wolff's law (Wolff, 1893; Frost, 2001).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to Wolff, 1893 and Frost, 2001.

claim: Rolvien et al. found that bone volume fraction (BV/TV) did not scale with body mass in three toothed whale species.
source: In fact, Rolvien et al. investigated characteristics of the vertebral bodies of three toothed whale species sperm whale, orca (Orcinus orca) and harbor porpoise (Phocoena phocoena) and found that bone volume fraction (BV/TV) did not scale with body mass
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rolvien et al., 2017.

claim: Rolvien et al. found that trabeculae were thicker and fewer in number in larger whale species.
source: but that trabeculae were thicker and fewer in number in larger whale species (Rolvien et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rolvien et al., 2017.

claim: Research has shown the relationship between bone microanatomical organization, habitats and locomotion patterns in different taxa.
source: Although research has shown the relationship between bone microanatomical organization, habitats and locomotion patterns in different taxa (Dumont et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dumont et al., 2013.

claim: The relationship between bone microanatomical organization and habitat/locomotion was less clear when comparing different species of whales.
source: this was less clear when comparing different species of whales, particularly in view of the variability of for example diving-depth behavior of the different animals (Rolvien et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rolvien et al., 2017.

claim: Histological sections of aquatic mammals displayed small islands of cartilaginous tissue embedded within the subchondral bone.
source: Interestingly, the histological sections of the aquatic mammals, displayed small islands of cartilaginous tissue embedded within the subchondral bone
evidence: This is supported by histological observations.

claim: In larger aquatic species such as the sperm whale, large islands of cartilage tissue were found deep in the trabecular bone.
source: and in the larger aquatic species, such as the sperm whale, large islands of cartilage tissue were found deep in the trabecular bone.
evidence: This is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The cartilage islands in aquatic mammals appeared to be composed of healthy cartilage-like tissue naturally embedded in the bone, devoid of evident signs of bone remodeling.
source: However, upon histological evaluation, these islands appeared to be composed of healthy cartilage-like tissue naturally embedded in the bone, devoid of evident signs of bone remodeling, not suggesting any form of pathology.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis.

claim: The cartilage islands in aquatic mammals may represent incomplete osteochondral ossification, similar to osteochondrosis in horses and other species.
source: The areas may, therefore, represent incomplete osteochondral ossification, well-known in the horse and other species as osteochondrosis (Thomas and Barnes, 2015; McCoy et al., 2013) similarly to what was found and described by Rolvien et al. in the central areas of the vertebrae of sperm whales (Rolvien et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to Thomas and Barnes, 2015; McCoy et al., 2013; Rolvien et al., 2017.

claim: The included aquatic species covered a wide range of body masses (from 54 to 48,000 kg).
source: However, the included aquatic species covered a wide range of body masses (from 54 to 48,000 kg)
evidence: This is supported by the species list in Table 1.

claim: The findings of the current study add significantly to our knowledge of the basic aspects of the biology of the osteochondral unit and clearly reflect the crucial influence of loading.
source: Taken together, the findings of the current study add significantly to our knowledge of the basic aspects of the biology of the osteochondral unit and clearly reflect the crucial influence of loading.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overall results of the study.

claim: All mammals have initially evolved on land and some of them returned to the water to become aquatic mammals.
source: We also know that all mammals have initially evolved on land and that some of them returned to the water to become what we now call aquatic mammals (Colbert and Morales, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Colbert and Morales, 2001.

claim: It is reasonable to assume that the osteochondral units of land-borne species from which current aquatic mammalian species evolved were similar to the common format of all currently existing terrestrial mammalian species.
source: Where we do not have histological data from the joints of the land-borne species from which our current aquatic mammalian species have evolved, it is reasonable to assume that their osteochondral units were similar to the common format of all currently existing terrestrial mammalian species.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on evolutionary principles.

claim: Accommodating loading is the most important evolutionary pressure on the osteochondral unit of terrestrial mammals.
source: The huge structural differences between the osteochondral units of the currently living aquatic and terrestrial mammals make hence clear that accommodating loading is the most important evolutionary pressure on the osteochondral unit of terrestrial mammals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparative structural differences observed in the study.

claim: The challenge of accommodating loading is dealt with by the architecture and structural composition of the osteochondral unit and not by molecular composition or cellular diversity.
source: Further, it highlights that this challenge is dealt with by the architecture and structural composition of the osteochondral unit and not by molecular composition or cellular diversity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that molecular and cellular components are similar while structural features differ.

claim: The specific tissue architecture and structural organization of especially the cartilage-bone interface got lost in aquatic mammals once the loading-based evolutionary pressure disappeared.
source: It is the specific tissue architecture and structural organization of especially the cartilage-bone interface that got lost in aquatic mammals, once the loading-based evolutionary pressure disappeared.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the evolutionary and structural observations.

claim: The study presents strong support for a recent call to rethink the current paradigms in articular cartilage regeneration.
source: In this sense, the study presents strong support for a recent call to rethink the current paradigms in articular cartilage regeneration (Malda et al., 2019)
evidence: This is an inference connecting the study findings to implications for regenerative medicine, supported by citation to Malda et al., 2019.

claim: Cartilage regeneration should focus on solutions with a proper architecture that allow restoration of biomechanical function, rather than on mere cellular activity in terms of production of extracellular matrix components.
source: through focusing on solutions with a proper architecture that allow restoration of (biomechanical) function, rather than on mere cellular activity in terms of production of extracellular matrix components.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings and represents speculative application to regenerative medicine.

claim: In total, tissue samples from 85 animals were harvested (34 for histological analysis, 29 for micro-CT and 20 for biomechanical analysis).
source: In total tissue samples from 85 animals (34 for histological analysis, 29 for micro-CT and 20 for biomechanical analysis) were harvested for a total of 15 different species.
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 caption.

claim: Samples were harvested from 15 different species.
source: In total tissue samples from 85 animals (34 for histological analysis, 29 for micro-CT and 20 for biomechanical analysis) were harvested for a total of 15 different species.
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 caption and shown in Table 1.

claim: Osteochondral tissue samples were harvested postmortem from the weight bearing central area of the humeral head of adult animals.
source: Osteochondral tissue samples were harvested postmortem from the weight bearing central area of the humeral head of adult animals sent for necropsy to the division of Pathology, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Utrecht University, in the Netherlands.
evidence: This describes the sampling methodology.

claim: Joints demonstrating macroscopic or microscopic signs of cartilage degeneration were excluded.
source: Joints demonstrating macroscopic or microscopic signs of cartilage degeneration were excluded
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Animals displaying signs of incomplete endochondral ossification were identified as skeletally immature and excluded.
source: animals displaying signs of incomplete endochondral ossification were identified as skeletally immature and excluded as well.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Stress relaxation tests were performed by first applying a pre-load of 0.01 N to test samples and then strained to 15% at a rate of 10 µm/s, followed by a relaxation period of 900 s.
source: Stress relaxation tests were performed by first applying a pre-load of 0.01 N to test samples and then strained to 15% at a rate of 10 µm/s, followed by a relaxation period of 900 s.
evidence: This describes the biomechanical testing methodology.

claim: All biomechanical tests were performed in PBS to approximate physiological conditions.
source: all tests were performed in PBS to approximate physiological conditions.
evidence: This describes the testing conditions for biomechanical analysis.

claim: Micro-CT images of the osteochondral cores were obtained with a micro-CT scanner with voxel size = 20 μm3.
source: Micro-CT images of the osteochondral cores were obtained with a micro-CT scanner (Quantum FX, Perkin Elmer, USA, voxel size = 20 μm3).
evidence: This describes the micro-CT imaging methodology.

claim: BoneJ software was used to determine the trabecular thickness (Tb.Th) and the bone volume fraction (Tb BV/TV).
source: BoneJ software (Doube et al., 2010) was used to determine the trabecular thickness (Tb.Th) and the bone volume fraction (Tb BV/TV) of the bone immediately underneath the cartilage (subchondral bone; determined as previously described Mancini et al., 2019), and at the center of the bone of the osteochondral cores (trabecular bone).
evidence: This describes the analysis methodology for micro-CT data, supported by citations to Doube et al., 2010 and Mancini et al., 2019.

claim: The level of statistical significance was set at p<0.05.
source: The level of statistical significance was set at p<0.05.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis methodology.
